rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s foretelling of future failures, Byzantine victory, and the Jews’ refusal to wish for death is among its signs beyond human capacity.
rows.anchor: والإعلان بالحوادث المستقبلة في الأعصار الآتية كقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On some reports, al-Kawthar denotes the Prophet’s abundant following and is one of four predictions embedded in the three verses of the sūra.
rows.anchor: إذا أريد به كما في بعض الروايات كثرة الإتباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading “wa-nḥar” as an order to sacrifice implicitly foretells the prosperity that would make the sacrifice possible.
rows.anchor: حيث أريد به كما هو الظاهر الأمر بالنحو فهو إشارة إلى اليسار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verse explicitly and implicitly predicts that the Prophet’s enemy, rather than the Prophet, will be cut off; this came to pass.
rows.anchor: حيث صرح ورمز بأن شانئك لا أنت أبتر لا عقب له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s rational coherence and precise meanings unite divine oneness, worship, law, exhortation, instruction, and moral guidance, placing each in its fitting position.
rows.anchor: لأنه اشتمل على توحيد الله تعالى وتنزيهه والدعاء إلى طاعته وبيان طرق عبادته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It joins proof to the claim being proved and uses subtle allusions, symbols, secrets, and wisdom to make obedience and avoidance more compelling.
rows.anchor: جامعا بين الحجة والمحتج له والدليل والمدلول عليه ليكون ذلك أوكد للزوم ما دعا إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the Quran’s distinction from scripture and the Prophet’s non-miraculous speech is as vast as the stars beyond a reaching hand, supporting his poetic comparison.
rows.anchor: فأين الثريا من يد المتناول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common view among most scholars makes the Quran’s supreme eloquence and clarity its central miracle.
rows.anchor: والمشهور عند الجمهور الاقتصار على بلاغته وفصاحته حيث بلغت الرتبة العليا والغاية القصوى

words: وأوحينا إلى أم موسى أن أرضعيه فإذا خفت عليه فألقيه في اليم ولا تخافي ولا تحزني إنا رادوه إليك وجاعلوه من المرسلين
rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: An unnamed woman answered al-Aṣmaʿī’s amazement at her poetry by citing the verse to Moses’ mother: it combines two commands, two prohibitions, and two glad tidings.
rows.anchor: أن الأصمعي وقف متعجبا من أمرأة تنشد شعرا فقالت أتعجب من هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars say the Quran’s distinctive arrangement is the specific locus of inimitability, while its other miraculous features follow from that form.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم جعل المدار النظم المخصوص والباقي تابع له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proponents of the arrangement theory argue that Quranic words are ordinary Arabic and many meanings occur in earlier books, while unseen knowledge is miraculous regardless of language or form.
rows.anchor: ولا بمعانيه فإن كثيرا منها موجود في الكتب المتقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author regards the distinctive-arrangement theory as close to the truth, though he signals that it has shortcomings.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم ما فيه وإن كان قريبا إلى الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects pure ṣarfa as the most remote explanation of inimitability, disapproves al-Murtaḍā’s version, and regards attributing the miracle to the Quran’s pre-eternity as still more remote.
rows.anchor: وأبعد الأقوال عندي كونه بالصرفة المحضة حتى أن قول المرتضى فيها غير مرتضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalam can mean the act of speaking or the utterance produced by it; linguistically the word primarily names the product, whether much or little and literal or figurative, though al-Raḍī notes its use for the act.
rows.anchor: ولفظ الكلام موضوع لغة لثاني قليلا كان أو كثيرا حقيقة كان أو حكما وقد يستعمل استعمال المصدر كما ذكره الرضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each sense has a verbal and a mental form: verbal speech is the act of the tongue or the quality of audible sound; mental speech is the mind’s unexpressed act or its imagined, internally ordered words.
rows.anchor: فعل الإنسان باللسان وما يساعده من المخارج

words: فأسرها يوسف في نفسه ولم يبدها لهم قال أنتم شر مكانا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Joseph verse, “قال” either substitutes for “أسر” or answers an implied question about what he said inwardly; both parses show mental speech as act and as content.
rows.anchor: بدل من ( أسر ) أو استئناف بياني كأنه قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses speak of inward secrets, remembering God inwardly, and what people say within themselves; in 3:167 that inward-speech reading is the most immediate sense.
rows.anchor: أي يقولون في أنفسهم كما هو الأسرع إنسياقا إلى الذهن والآيات في ذلك كثيرة

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarānī reports from Umm Salama that a man asked the Prophet about an inward thought he feared would ruin his reward; the Prophet called it speech and said only a believer receives it.
rows.anchor: ما رواه الطبراني عن أم سلمة أنها سمعت رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sacred hadith saying God remembers the servant who remembers Him inwardly supports mental speech in both its act and content senses, for servant and Lord, while their realities remain incomparable.
rows.anchor: فإن ذكرني في نفسه ذكرته في نفسي الحديث وفيه دليل على أن للعبد كلاما نفسيا بالمعنيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s mental speech in its first sense is an eternal attribute opposed to an inner defect like muteness, not made of letters or words, and one in essence despite varied objects of relation.
rows.anchor: صفة أزلية منافية للآفة الباطنية التي هي بمنزلة الخرس في التكلم الإنساني اللفظي ليس من جنس الحروف والألفاظ أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relation of divine speech to a newly occurring object does not make the attribute itself temporal; the author accepts renewal only in the relation’s occurrence.
rows.anchor: والتعلق من الأمور النسبية التي لا يضر تجددها وحدوث المتعلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The excerpt lists possible sevenfold divisions such as clear and ambiguous, abrogating and abrogated, general and particular, narratives, commands, prohibitions, promises, and guidance; it says these are plausible but lack evidence for privileging one.
rows.anchor: وخصوص وعموم وقصص وقيل : إظهار الربوبية وإثبات الوحدانية

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: The view that the seven aḥruf are seven dialects is attributed to Thaʿlab, Abū ʿUbayd, al-Azharī, and others; Ibn ʿAṭiyya chose it and al-Bayhaqī authenticated it.
rows.anchor: وإليه ذهب ثعلب وأبو عبيد والأزهري وآخرون واختاره ابن عطية وصححه البيهقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To answer the objection that Arabic has more than seven dialects, proponents say the count means the most eloquent: Quraysh, Hudhayl, Tamim, Azd, Rabiʿa, Hawazin, and Saʿd b. Bakr.
rows.anchor: واعترض بأن لغات العرب أكثر وأجيب بأن المراد أفصحها وهي لغة قريش وهذيل وتميم والأزد

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba rejects the dialect theory because the Quran was revealed only in Quraysh’s language, citing the rule that each messenger speaks his people’s language.
rows.anchor: لم ينزل القرآن إلا بلغة قريش بدليل

rows.speaker: أبو علي الأهوازي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Ahwāzī resolves Ibn Qutayba’s objection by locating the seven dialects within Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وعليه يلتزم كون السبع في بطون قريش وبه جزم أبو علي الأهوازي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven dialects need not apply to every word; rather, they are distributed through the Quran, with some dialectal forms more prominent than others.
rows.anchor: وليس المراد أن كل كلمة تقرأ على سبع لغات بل أنها مفرقة فيه

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Another view confines the seven dialects to Mudar, based on ʿUmar’s statement; some proponents identify them as Hudhayl, Kināna, Qays, Ḍabba, Taym al-Ribāb, Asad b. Khuzayma, and Quraysh.
rows.anchor: السبع في مضر خاصة لقول عمر رضي الله عنه : نزل القرآن بلغة مضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further account says revelation began in Quraysh and neighboring eloquent tribes, then the Prophet permitted dialectal recitation to relieve hardship and tribal resistance, based on what he transmitted rather than personal choice.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنزل أولا بلسان قريش ومن جاورهم من الفصحاء ثم أبيح للعرب أن تقرأه بلغاتها دفعا للمشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this account, Gabriel brought one aḥruf to the Prophet at each presentation until the full revelation was complete.
rows.anchor: في كل عرضة بحرف إلى أن تمت

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyūṭī rejects the dialect explanation: ʿUmar and Hishām were both Qurashī yet recited differently, so ʿUmar’s objection cannot concern a dialect difference; the seven aḥruf mean something else.
rows.anchor: هو مردود بأن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه وهشام بن حكيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says this rebuttal attacks a claim no Muslim made: that tribes could arbitrarily rewrite revelation in their dialects; the readings instead reflect revealed forms transmitted beyond a Companion’s own dialect.
rows.anchor: أدعى أحد من المسلمين أن معنى إنزال القرآن على هذه السبع من لغات هؤلاء العرب أنه أنزل كيفما كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For al-Ālūsī, differing Companion readings and their transmission across tribal dialects show that the aḥruf rest on prophetic narration rather than a reader’s dialect knowledge; he favors the seven-dialect account.
rows.anchor: كل ذلك يدل على أن مرجع السبع الرواية لا الدراية فرد الإمام السيوطي لا أدري ماذا أرد منه

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī begins his discussion of Quran collection by saying it was first collected in the Prophet’s presence, citing al-Ḥākim with a chain meeting the criteria of al-Bukhārī and Muslim from Zayd b. Thābit.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج الحاكم بسند على شرط الشيخين عن زيد بن ثابت

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila agree that God’s being a speaker means He creates speech, with no real attribute accruing to Him, and that divine speech is created, composed of letters and sounds.
rows.anchor: أما المعتزلة فاتفقوا كافة على أن معنى كونه تعالى متكلما أنه خالق الكلام

rows.speaker: الجبائي وأبو هاشم
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī and his son Abū Hāshim hold that divine speech is originated in a locus.
rows.anchor: الجبائي وإبنه أبو هاشم إلى أنه حادث في محل

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī further says God creates speech for Himself at each reciter’s place of recitation; the other Muʿtazilites disagree.
rows.anchor: يحدث عند قراءة كل قاريء كلاما لنفسه في محل القراءة وخالفه الباقون

rows.speaker: أبو الهذيل بن العلاف
rows.claim: Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and his followers place some divine speech in a locus, such as “Be,” while commands, prohibitions, reports, and questions are not in a locus.
rows.anchor: وذهب أبو الهذيل بن العلاف وأصحابه إلى أن بعضه في محل وهو قوله كن وبعضه لا في محل

rows.speaker: الحسن بن محمد النجار
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan b. Muḥammad al-Najjār says God’s speech is an accident when recited and a body when written.
rows.anchor: الحسن بن محمد النجار إلى ان كلام الباري إذا قريء فهو عرض وإذا كتب فهو جسم

rows.speaker: الإمامية والخوارج والحشوية
rows.claim: The Imāmiyya, Khārijites, and Ḥashwiyya also describe divine speech as composed of letters and sounds, though they differ on its status.
rows.anchor: وذهبت الإمامية والخوارج والحشوية إلى أن كلام الرب تعالى مركب من الحروف والأصوات

rows.speaker: الحشوية
rows.claim: The Ḥashwiyya regard the letter-and-sound speech as eternal and subsisting in God; some make it like human speech, while others distinguish eternal from originated letters and sounds.
rows.anchor: لكن منهم من زعم أنه من جنس كلام البشر

rows.speaker: الكرامية
rows.claim: The Karrāmiyya say “speech” means either the capacity to speak, which is eternal and singular, or utterances, which are temporal and multiple; both subsist in God.
rows.anchor: وأما الكرامية فقالوا إن الكلام قد يطلق على القدرة على التكلم وقد يطلق على الأقوال والعبارات

rows.speaker: الواقفية
rows.claim: The Wāqifiyya agree that divine speech came to be after not existing, but differ over whether to call it eternal or created; some avoid “created” while calling it originated.
rows.anchor: وأما الواقفية فقد أجمعوا على أن كلام الرب تعالى كائن بعد أن لم يكن

rows.speaker: بعض القائلين بالحدوث
rows.claim: Some who hold divine speech originated say it is neither a substance nor an accident.
rows.anchor: ومن القائلين بالحدوث من قال ليس جوهرا ولا عرضا

rows.speaker: بعض المعترفين بالصانع
rows.claim: Some who acknowledge a Creator deny that He can be described as speaking, whether by speech or without speech.
rows.anchor: وذهب بعض المعترفين بالصانع إلى أنه لا يوصف بكونه متكلما لا بكلام ولا بغير كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute arises from two apparently conflicting syllogisms: speech is God’s attribute and attributes are eternal, but ordered successive letters are temporal.
rows.anchor: وكل ما هو صفة له فهو قديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One camp makes God’s letter-and-sound speech eternal and denies that every composition of letters and sounds must be temporal; al-Ālūsī says false claims have been attributed to them.
rows.anchor: فقوم ذهبوا إلى أن كلامه تعالى حروف وأصوات وهي قديمة ومنعوا أن كل ما هو مؤلف من حروف وأصوات فهو حادث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another camp treats speech as temporal sounds and letters subsisting in another locus, such as a tablet or Gabriel, and defines God as speaker by His producing them there.
rows.anchor: وآخرون قالوا بحدوث كلامه تعالى وأنه مؤلف من أصوات وحروف وهو قائم بغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further camp makes speech a temporal attribute of God composed of letters and sounds, denying that every attribute of God must be eternal.
rows.anchor: واللغة ذهبوا إلى أن كلامه تعالى صفة له مؤلفة من الحروف والأصوات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group says divine speech is one simple meaning subsisting in God and denies that it is composed of letters and sounds.
rows.anchor: كلامه تعالى معنى واحد بسيط قائم بذاته تعالى فهم منعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some thinkers, overwhelmed by the dispute, suspend judgment and leave the matter unresolved.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم تحير فوقف وحبس ذهنه في مسجد الدهشة واعتكف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says both syllogisms are sound and both conclusions true, since different circumstances call for different accounts of speech.
rows.anchor: وعندي القياسان صحيحان والنتيجتان صادقتان ولكل مقام مقال ولكل كلام أحوال

rows.speaker: الزجاج واللحياني
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and al-Liḥyānī say the word Quran was transferred into a personal proper name, as al-Shāfiʿī and leading legal theorists also hold; on this account it resists ordinary genus-based definition.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج واللحياني لكنه نقل وجعل علما شخصيا كما ذهب إليه الشافعي ومحققو الأصوليين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed definition calls the Quran speech revealed to establish inimitability by even one sūra; al-Ghazālī defines it as what is transmitted with mass attestation between the covers of the codex.
rows.anchor: ولعل من عرفه بالكلام المنزل للإعجاز بسورة منه أراد تصوير مفهوم لفظ القرآن وكذا من قال كالغزالي أنه ما نقل بين دفتي المصحف تواترا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The codex-based definition distinguishes canonical text from recitation abrogated while its ruling remains and from non-mutawātir material, which do not ground recitation or purity rulings.
rows.anchor: ومما لم ينقل كالمنسوخ تلاوته نحو إنا أنزلنا المال لإقام الصلاة وإيتاء الزكاة وما نقل ولم يتواتر نحو ثلاثة أيام متتابعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inimitability definition is circular and insufficient: inimitability is not an evident essential trait known to all, and identifying a sūra as part of the Quran already presupposes knowing the Quran.
rows.anchor: أن كونه للإعجاز ليس لازما بينا إذ لا يعرفه إلا الأفراد من العلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The codex definition is likewise circular because recognizing the codex depends on knowing the Quran that is written in it.
rows.anchor: معرفة المصحف موقوفة على معرفة القرآن إذ ليس هو إلا ما كتب فيه القرآن

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: The Sufis read the Quran as a sign of the divine Essence in which attributes are effaced, the manifestation of oneness revealed to Muhammad so that unity becomes witnessed in the cosmos.
rows.anchor: أن القرآن إشارة إلى الذات التي يضمحل بها جميع الصفات فهي المجلي المسمى بالأحدية

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: They interpret the Quran’s descent as the complete manifestation of absolute oneness in Muhammad, with nothing withheld, and its description as noble reflects this incomparable generosity.
rows.anchor: ومعنى هذا الإنزال أن الحقيقة الأحدية المتعالية في ذراها ظهرت فيه صلى الله عليه وسلم بكمالها

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: They take “the wise Quran” as divine realities that the servant realizes and ascends through step by step; the ascent continues as God’s self-disclosure continues.
rows.anchor: وأما القرآن الحكيم فهوية الحقائق الإلهية يعرج العبد بالتحقيق بها في الذات شيئا فشيئا

words: ولقد آتيناك سبعا من المثاني والقرآن العظيم
rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: They interpret the “great Quran” as the totality of the divine Essence in absolute oneness, encompassing every rank, attribute, and aspect; the seven repetitions signify the seven attributes realized in the Prophet.
rows.anchor: فهو إشارة إلى الجملة الذاتية لا باعتبار النزول ولا باعتبار المكانة بل مطلق الأحدية الذاتية

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: They interpret the Merciful’s teaching of the Quran as a merciful self-disclosure that gives the servant a Quranic knowing and delight; God is known only through His names and attributes.
rows.anchor: فهو إشارة إلى أن العبد إذا تجلى عليه الرحمن وجد لذة رحمانية تكسبه معرفة قرآنية

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: For them, the Furqan signifies the diverse realities of divine names and attributes, whose distinctions include Beneficent and Avenger, pleasure and wrath.
rows.anchor: وأما الفرقان عندهم فإشارة إلى حقيقة الأسماء والصفات على اختلاف تنوعاتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names and attributes have differing ranks in excellence, not because any is deficient; the cited prophetic prayer seeks refuge in mercy, pleasure, and God from their counterparts.
rows.anchor: فكانت المعافاة أفضل من العقوبة والرضا أفضل من السخط فأعاذه بالفاضل مما يليه

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd says he recognized God through His joining opposites.
rows.anchor: أبو سعيد : عرفت الله تعالى بجمعه بين الضدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As manifestation of both Quran and Furqan, Muhammad is the seal of prophets and leader of messengers: nothing needed was omitted, leaving later prophets no further perfection to announce.
rows.anchor: ولكونه صلى الله عليه وسلم مظهرا للقرآن والفرقان كان خاتم النبيين وإمام المرسلين لأنه ما ترك شيئا يحتاج إليه

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: Another Sufi formulation equates Quran and Furqan with the stations of union and distinction: a perfected servant needs both, since distinction is required for servitude and union for gnosis.
rows.anchor: إشارتان إلى مقام الجمع والفرق بأقسامها قالوا ولا بد للعبد الكامل منهما

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: Union means witnessing things through God and disclaiming one’s own power; union-of-union is complete absorption and annihilation of everything besides God.
rows.anchor: والجمع عندهم شهود الأشياء بالله تعالى والتبري من الحول والقوة إلا بالله وجمع الجمع الاستهلاك بالكلية

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: The first distinction veils the servant from God through creation; the second sees creation standing through God and unity within multiplicity without either obscuring the other.
rows.anchor: وهو شهود قيام الخلق بالحق ورؤية الوحدة في الكثرة

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: “Distinction of attribute” is the absolute Essence appearing through its attributes; “distinction of union” is the One appearing in many stations, which are only conceptual relations until the One manifests through them.
rows.anchor: وفرق الوصف وهو ظهور الذات الأحدية بأوصافها في الحضرة الواحدة وفرق الجمع وهو تكثر الواحد بظهوره في المراتب

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: Sufis call the Quran comprehensive, implicit knowledge of all realities and the Furqan detailed knowledge separating truth from falsehood.
rows.anchor: وكثيرا ما يطلقون القرآن على العلم اللدني الإجمالي الجامع للحقائق كلها والفرقان على العلم التفصيلي الفارق بين الحق والباطل

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī says the Quran contains the Furqan, but the Furqan does not contain the Quran: details exist within the comprehensive whole, not vice versa, so the Quran was uniquely given to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: أن القرآن يتضمن الفرقان والفرقان لايتضمن القرآن لأن تفاصيل المراتب
